title: You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings

problem.summary: Detection systems repurpose classifiers and run multi-stage pipelines (proposals, feature extraction, classification, post-processing) whose components are trained separately, making them slow, hard to optimize, and short of real-time performance.
statements: Multi-stage detection pipelines are slow and hard to optimize because each component must be trained separately.
Region-proposal detectors such as Fast/Faster R-CNN fall short of real-time performance even after speed-ups.
Classifier-based pipelines cannot be optimized end-to-end for the final detection metric.

evidence.quote: These complex pipelines are slow and hard to optimize because each individual component must be trained separately.
Each stage of this complex pipeline must be precisely tuned independently and the resulting system is very slow, taking more than 40 seconds per image at test time [14].
While they offer speed and accuracy improvements over R-CNN, both still fall short of real-time performance.

background.summary: The paper compares against DPM sliding-window detection, the R-CNN/Fast R-CNN/Faster R-CNN proposal-based lineage, Deep MultiBox, OverFeat and MultiGrasp, arguing that all of them keep detection as a disjoint pipeline rather than a single jointly trained network.

relatedWork.name: R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: prior proposal-based pipeline; slow, stages tuned independently
relatedWork.quote: Selective Search [35] generates potential bounding boxes, a convolutional network extracts features, an SVM scores the boxes, a linear model adjusts the bounding boxes, and non-max suppression eliminates duplicate detections.

relatedWork.name: Fast R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: top-performing detector used for error analysis and model combination
relatedWork.quote: Fast R-CNN, a top detection method [14], mistakes background patches in an image for objects because it can’t see the larger context.

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: neural proposal competitor; more accurate but slower variants
relatedWork.quote: The VGG-16 version of Faster R-CNN is 10 mAP higher but is also 6 times slower than YOLO.

relatedWork.name: DPM
relatedWork.relation: sliding-window baseline; disjoint pipeline of static features and classifiers
relatedWork.quote: Our system replaces all of these disparate parts with a single convolutional neural network.

relatedWork.name: OverFeat
relatedWork.relation: prior localizer adapted to detection; disjoint and context-free
relatedWork.quote: OverFeat cannot reason about global context and thus requires significant post-processing to produce coherent detections.

evidence.quote: Current detection systems repurpose classifiers to perform detection.
After classification, post-processing is used to refine the bounding boxes, eliminate duplicate detections, and rescore the boxes based on other objects in the scene [13].

solution.summary: YOLO casts detection as a single regression problem from image pixels to bounding box coordinates and class probabilities: one convolutional network predicts all boxes and classes for an S x S grid in one evaluation, trained end-to-end on detection loss.
solution.approach: The image is split into an S x S grid whose cells predict B boxes with confidences and C conditional class probabilities, decoded at test time into class-specific scores and filtered with non-max suppression.
components: S x S grid with per-cell bounding box and class probability predictions (7 x 7 x 30 output for PASCAL VOC)
GoogLeNet-inspired network with 24 convolutional and 2 fully connected layers
Fast YOLO variant with 9 convolutional layers
multi-part sum-squared error loss with lambda_coord = 5 and lambda_noobj = 0.5
single responsible predictor per object chosen by highest current IOU
ImageNet pretraining at 224 x 224 then fine-tuning at 448 x 448

evidence.quote: We reframe object detection as a single regression problem, straight from image pixels to bounding box coordinates and class probabilities.
Our system divides the input image into an S × S grid.
A single convolutional network simultaneously predicts multiple bounding boxes and class probabilities for those boxes.
Our network has 24 convolutional layers followed by 2 fully connected layers.
Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance.

experiments.summary: YOLO is compared with real-time and non-real-time detectors on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012, its errors are broken down against Fast R-CNN (including rescoring Fast R-CNN with YOLO), and generalization is tested on the Picasso and People-Art artwork datasets.

evidence.quote: Fast YOLO is the fastest object detection method on PASCAL; as far as we know, it is the fastest extant object detector.
With 52.7% mAP, it is more than twice as accurate as prior work on real-time detection.
On the VOC 2012 test set, YOLO scores 57.9% mAP.

limitations.summary: YOLO trades accuracy for speed: localization is its dominant error source, the grid imposes strong spatial limits that hurt dense/small objects, coarse features limit box precision, and VOC 2012 mAP trails the proposal-based state of the art.
items: Strong spatial constraints (two boxes, one class per grid cell) limit the number of nearby objects the model can detect.
Small objects appearing in groups (e.g. flocks of birds) are handled poorly.
Learned box shapes generalize poorly to new or unusual aspect ratios and configurations.
Multiple downsampling layers leave relatively coarse features for box prediction.
The sum-squared loss weights errors in small and large boxes equally, though small-box errors hurt IOU more.
Localization errors dominate: incorrect localizations are the main source of error.
VOC 2012 mAP (57.9%) is below the proposal-based state of the art.

evidence.quote: YOLO imposes strong spatial constraints on bounding box predictions since each grid cell only predicts two boxes and can only have one class.
Our model struggles with small objects that appear in groups, such as flocks of birds.
Our main source of error is incorrect localizations.
Our system struggles with small objects compared to its closest competitors.

equations.name: multi-part detection loss
equations.expr: sum of lambda_coord box-coordinate terms + confidence terms (lambda_noobj for no-object cells) + class probability terms

applications.detail: The introduction motivates fast accurate detection as a way to let computers drive cars without specialized sensors.
applications.quote: Fast, accurate algorithms for object detection would allow computers to drive cars without specialized sensors, enable assistive devices to convey real-time scene information to human users, and unlock the potential for general purpose, responsive robotic systems.

applications.detail: Real-time scene information for human users and responsive robotic systems are named as target applications.
applications.quote: enable assistive devices to convey real-time scene information to human users

applications.detail: A webcam-connected demo sustained real-time detection including image fetch and display time, functioning like a tracking system.
applications.quote: YOLO is a fast, accurate object detector, making it ideal for computer vision applications.

deploymentClaims: Base YOLO runs at 45 FPS with no batch processing on a Titan X GPU.
Fast YOLO runs at more than 150 FPS (155 FPS reported in Table 1).
Streaming video can be processed in real time with less than 25 ms of latency.
Pretrained models and training/testing code are open source.

evidence.quote: Our base network runs at 45 frames per second with no batch processing on a Titan X GPU and a fast version runs at more than 150 fps.
This means we can process streaming video in real-time with less than 25 milliseconds of latency.
All of our training and testing code is open source.
